foreignObject.h5:div: If the term is unfamiliar to you, here is the short version: System 1 is the fast, intuitive, and emotional system, while
System 2 is the slow, deliberate, and logical one. Daniel Kahneman, Nobel Prize laureate in Economics, coined this
term in his psychology work on judgment and decision making, which challenged the idea that humans are rational
TypeSafe leaned into this and named their new type of classification models “System-One Models”, in contrast to
text-generating Large Language Models (LLMs), which are more like System 2. Jev is their first System-One model
How do they compare to LLMs?
LLMs work by predicting the most probable next token, step by step. Especially for machine-to-machine
communication, people have tried to squeeze LLM output into a schema. There are techniques for that, but they limit
the model in its reasoning capabilities
, and they are nowhere near efficient
enough for realtime applications at a feasible cost.
So what does Jev do differently? It takes the same input as basic LLMs (which is plain text) and a set of questions
with their answer candidates. Its output is then a set of probabilities for each question. The model fundamentally
does not generate text and therefore cannot return an answer outside the supplied schema.
That reliability and efficiency make it a good fit for realtime applications.
Oh, and they are really really cheap. Jev is currently listed at 0.0047€ per 1M input tokens, with output tokens being
free. TypeSafe attributes this price to the massive parallelism of its decision heads.
Despite Jev having been released only on September 15th, open-weight alternatives have sprouted up like
mushrooms. They mostly work by architecturally modifying and fine-tuning a pre-trained language model on a
specific dataset. Since the problem space is less fragmented, way smaller models get acceptable results.
TypeSafe AI claims not to train on your data
For highly sensitive applications, like handling health data, this is not enough. Open-weight models can be self-
hosted, which gives the operator more control over where inference data goes. It does not guarantee that the
whole application keeps no data off-premises.
- 4B params, the open-weight benchmark leader when I started this experiment
- ~500MB size, less than 50ms latency even on CPU, often requires fine-tuning
Operating rooms have lots of equipment, and each device brings its own controls. A voice assistant could save you
the constant reaching for knobs and menus. But a natural command is not enough on its own. The system has to
identify which device and setting the speaker means, handle values precisely, and avoid changing anything the
speaker did not ask to change.

There are a lot of complex components involved to make this work reliably in the real world. Luckily, the virtual room
simplifies things greatly and allows us to focus on the narrow question of whether a System-One model can turn
short utterances into actionable commands we can automatically apply to the objects in the room.
The API gives the model the current state, the utterance, and questions about possible actions to modify the fields/
attributes of the objects in the room.
System-One question types and example outputs.
questions in the API. The possible answers are predetermined by the application, read more on that

is very important, as it cannot name an

, running the model locally is important for GDPR compliance. The
less hardware is required, the easier it is to set up for institutions, especially hospitals. So naturally I wanted to try out
how far we can get with one.
JevK5 has a model version with 2B parameters that can somehow run on my RTX 2080. The server exposes a
System-One-compatible API, so the surrounding request format stays close to the hosted Jev example. I use the
model and package revision shown in

In the recorded runs, Jev performs better than JevK5-2B on utterance-level accuracy. Jev also performs better in the
rolling evaluation, where predictions are applied through an utterance sequence and earlier mistakes can affect later
state. I keep these measurements separate because JevK5-2B has fewer evaluated cases. The paired comparison in

There may be a dataset issue here too. I discovered cases where an utterance like “tilt table by 5 degrees” has an

per utterance. That is more than enough to count as real-time
interaction. The average human response time is around 200ms, which is excluding the time to physically execute
the command, so Jev does not lag behind.
“It runs locally” and “it is useful locally” are two different pairs of shoes.
. So the local model ran on my RTX 2080, but this particular 2B
configuration was not fast enough for the near-real-time interaction I had in mind.
System-One’s constrained outputs are an appealing interface for equipment-control software. The schema narrows
what the model can return, and the API scores each field directly. That is a much better contract than parsing free-
JevK5-2B did not turn out to be a practical local substitute for Jev in this setup. It was less accurate and much
slower, and both models missed nearly every positive safety-interlock case. If privacy is the reason to run locally, it
currently costs more accuracy and latency than I would accept.
So no, local System-One control is not ready. But the failure modes I saw could be explained by sub-optimal data and
instruction setup. Next steps are to investigate whether better data and more guardrails can close the gap without
JevK5-2B runs the default checkpoint. I did not tune it, I just pointed the server at it. My
bet is that fine-tuning on messier utterances, ambiguous phrasing, field boundary cases and background noise
buys more than swapping architectures. That needs human-reviewed labels instead of the generated ones I used,
which would also make the benchmark mean more than “it works on my generated test set”.
The RTX 2080 is what I had, not what I would buy for this. A newer card, or a smaller or quantized
checkpoint, would probably bring latency into a comfortable range. Whether that gets below the ~200 ms human
response time on hardware a hospital would actually buy, I have not tested.
Rule-based field validation and abstention on low confidence were cheap to add,
and they catch the errors the schema lets through on its own. That being said, corrective measures could make a
lot of sense in addition to those.
Almeida, Diogo. “Introducing System-One Models and Jev.” Accessed October 10, 2026.
